name: Pingelapese
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Pingelapese is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Kennedy 2002 'Stress and reduplication in the Ponapeic languages' (GLOW 25), is a conference talk with no published or posted text: the Meertens programme page (archived) confirms the talk and links an abstract PDF that was never captured and is now 404; Kennedy's 2017 CV lists it as a presentation only; his archived UCSB paper page and current page carry no copy; Its content is presumably subsumed by Kennedy 2003 (diss., held by the project), which gives only a family-level right-edge / alternating-mora stress generalization (pp. 36-37) and, for Pingilapese, a model prediction of strictly alternating moraic stress (p. 142) with no stressed forms. Good & Welley 1989 (p. 6) explicitly leaves Pingilapese stress for further research; Hattori 2012 and Ehmes 2005 are silent; Kennedy 2002 WCCFL 21 never mentions Pingilapese. No first-hand Pingelapese word-stress statement exists in anything read. Acquisition targets: Rehg 1993 'Proto-Micronesian prosody' (family-level, print/restricted) - medium; the GLOW abstract itself - medium at best, low expected yield.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is always attracted to the right edges of words, with secondary stress assigned alternatingly towards the left. [...] In languages with full deletion patterns, like Pohnpeian, Mokilese, and Marshallese, primary stress occurs on the final surface vowel. In those with an incomplete vowel-weakening process (either as devoicing, or deletion of a subset of vowels), primary stress occurs on the penultimate mora. (pp. 36-37) / [Pingilapese:] The system predicts stress to occur strictly on alternating moras (pp. 141-142)
new_statements.citation: Kennedy, Robert (2003). Confluence in phonology: Evidence from Micronesian reduplication. PhD dissertation, University of Arizona (ROA 606).
new_statements.locator: §2.3.1.2 Stress, pp. 36-37; §5.3.4 Pingilapese: a summary, pp. 141-142
new_statements.reading: NOT a first-hand description of Pingelapese. It is a Micronesian family-level generalization (after Rehg 1993): primary stress at the right edge, secondary stress on alternating moras leftward; the exact locus (final surface vowel vs penultimate mora) depends on whether final-vowel deletion is complete, and Kennedy names Pohnpeian, Mokilese and Marshallese but never places Pingilapese in either class. The only Pingilapese-specific line is an OT-model prediction (strict alternating-mora stress) derived from Good & Welley 1989 data that carry no stress marks. The sole primary source (Good & Welley 1989, p. 6) says stress was not investigated; Hattori 2012 and Ehmes 2005 are silent. So Pingelapese still has no first-hand word-stress statement; best available coding would be 'right-edge / alternating moraic, locus unspecified' at family level, flagged as inferred. Rehg 1993 (Proto-Micronesian prosody, OL Special Publication 24; not reached, archive.org lending copy restricted) is the source to acquire if a family-level statement is to be used.

sources.locator: §2.3.1.2 Stress, pp. 36-37; §5.3.4 Pingilapese: a summary, pp. 141-142
sources.note: Family-level statement (§2.3.1.2, pp. 36-37, citing Rehg 1993): primary stress attracted to the right word edge, secondary stress alternating leftward at the mora level; in full final-vowel-deletion languages (Pohnpeian, Mokilese, Marshallese named; Pingilapese not named) primary stress is on the final surface vowel, in incomplete-weakening languages on the penultimate mora. For Pingilapese specifically (§5.3.4, pp. 141-142) only a prediction of the shared OT hierarchy: 'The system predicts stress to occur strictly on alternating moras'; no stressed Pingilapese forms are given anywhere in §5.…

sources.quote: Further research on the Pingilapese sound system would include research on the topics of stress, intonation, word breaks, consonant releases word finally, and the presence of possible transitional vowels.
sources.note: Section 1 'Sounds and spelling' gives phonemes, allophones and contrasts only; p. 6 explicitly lists stress among topics left for 'further research'. No stress statement. (The 'word stress is on the penultimate syllable' line at p. 131 of the same volume is Good's Kosraean paper quoting Lee 1975, not Pingelapese.)
